title: Doomsday

jokes.text: Andy sings 'Closing Time' as an end-of-day office tradition, belting it out while employees look on with varying degrees of tolerance
jokes.setup: Andy has established a daily end-of-day tradition of singing 'Closing Time'
jokes.punchline: The sheer earnestness of Andy singing a Semisonic song as a mandatory workplace ritual is inherently cringeworthy and absurd
jokes.explanation: Deeply Andy-specific — his need for approval and forced fun is baked into every note he sings. The running gag of him being the only one enthusiastic is strong character comedy.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head: 'Andy has been manager for 105 days, which means I've heard Closing Time 105 times. Still don't know the words.'
jokes.setup: The 'Closing Time' tradition has apparently been going on every single workday
jokes.punchline: Despite 105 repetitions, Jim still doesn't know the words — implying he's actively tuned it out every single time
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — two sentences convey 105 days of suffering and complete psychological disengagement. The punchline (still don't know the words) is the perfect Jim Halpert move: passive resistance so total he won't even absorb a song he's heard over a hundred times.

jokes.text: Andy storms off: 'You know what? Fine! I try to start fun traditions for you guys but if you don't want to sing, no traditions.' Then immediately turns back and sings the outro.
jokes.setup: Andy threatens to end the tradition because no one is singing along
jokes.punchline: He can't even quit his own tradition — he immediately resumes singing the song's ending, undercutting his own tantrum
jokes.explanation: This is the best beat of the cold open — Andy's lack of self-control is perfectly character-specific. He threatens to withhold the tradition as punishment, then immediately surrenders to his own compulsion. Strong structural irony.

jokes.text: Pam's talking head: 'I never heard that song before and once I heard it I did not care for it. But that song means it's time to go home. Now it's my favourite song.'
jokes.setup: Pam initially hated Closing Time
jokes.punchline: Pure Pavlovian conditioning — she now loves the song purely as a stimulus for leaving work, not for any musical merit
jokes.explanation: A neat three-act beat in two sentences. The pivot from 'did not care for it' to 'now it's my favourite song' is delivered with perfect Office-style matter-of-factness. Good closing cap on the cold open running gag.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head dream: 'Last night I dreamed that the number two was the most valued number in the world. The Vice President had all the power, athletes fought for silver medals, women were considered the best gender. And stadiums of fans shouted, "We're number two!"'
jokes.setup: Dwight describes a dream that reflects his anxieties about being a number two/assistant
jokes.punchline: The dream's internal logic is completely consistent and escalates beautifully — each example more absurd than the last, culminating in 'women were considered the best gender' as a throwaway in the list
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the episode. The dream is a perfect encapsulation of Dwight's psychology — his obsession with hierarchy and being second-in-command — rendered through absurdist logic that holds together beautifully. 'Women were considered the best gender' lands as a bizarre throwaway that doubles back to make satirical sense within the internal logic. The stadium chant is a perfect button. Comparable in craft to an 8.0 anchor — the character integration pushes it slightly higher.

jokes.text: Dwight's kicker: 'As with all my dreams, I'm guessing it was about my fear of immigrants.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has just described an elaborate dream about wanting to be number two
jokes.punchline: He dismisses the obvious psychological reading (insecurity about status) and replaces it with a completely unrelated and darkly absurd conclusion about immigrants
jokes.explanation: The button on the dream sequence is arguably better than the dream itself. 'As with all my dreams' implies this is a recurring interpretive framework for Dwight — that every dream he has gets routed back to immigrants. The deadpan confidence of the non-sequitur is perfectly Dwight. Extremely quotable. A strong 8+ moment.

jokes.text: Robert calls Kevin and Oscar 'Tweedle-Dee and Tweedle-Dum' then clarifies: 'Who are they? They're both Kevin.'
jokes.setup: Robert blames accounting for the mistake and uses the nursery rhyme insult
jokes.punchline: He immediately undermines the metaphor by noting both roles are Kevin — a dig at Kevin's competence so total that Oscar doesn't even warrant his own Tweedle
jokes.explanation: Sharp construction — the self-correction that turns a standard insult into a more specific and cutting one. Robert's willingness to clarify his own metaphor at Kevin's expense is excellent character work.

jokes.text: Robert describes Oscar as 'the Sex and the City gang' and struggles to describe Angela: 'Angela, if you can...'
jokes.setup: Robert is assigning pop-culture labels to his accounting team
jokes.punchline: He trails off on Angela as if even he can't find a cultural reference to contain her severity, giving up mid-sentence
jokes.explanation: The 'Sex and the City gang' as a label for Oscar is a solid character read. The Angela trailing off is funny but underdeveloped — the joke is that she's unclassifiable, but it doesn't fully land without a punchline.

jokes.text: Angela's flat response to Robert: 'Andy, sometimes I feel like you don't know me at all.' Followed by Andy: 'I would agree with that.'
jokes.setup: Robert lumps Angela in with a vague pop-culture reference she presumably rejects
jokes.punchline: Angela's wounded dignity is undercut by Andy immediately and cheerfully agreeing he doesn't know her
jokes.explanation: The two-beat exchange works well — Angela's self-important complaint sets up Andy's breezy obliviousness. His agreement is genuinely funny in its guilelessness.

jokes.text: Robert: 'Our favourite names, silly made-up names, normal names said in a silly voice. Wouldn't that be nice?'
jokes.setup: Robert promises that if mistakes are eliminated, they can spend meeting time talking about names
jokes.punchline: The escalating specificity of what name-talk they'd enjoy ('silly made-up names,' 'normal names said in a silly voice') reveals Robert's bizarre inner life beneath his executive exterior
jokes.explanation: A quintessential Robert California moment — he dangles a completely unhinged reward ('normal names said in a silly voice') with the gravity of a CEO promising bonuses. The earnest 'Wouldn't that be nice?' sells it completely.

jokes.text: Robert's exit line: 'And you can't have a favourite Iron Chef. It depends entirely on the secret ingredient. Sometimes I feel you don't know food at all.'
jokes.setup: Robert opened the meeting with the Iron Chef question; now he closes by answering it on his own terms
jokes.punchline: He returns to the Iron Chef question as a callback, but the punchline is that his 'answer' is actually a rebuke — you can't have a favourite. He makes food philosophy into a power move.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback structure — the Iron Chef question bookends his entire visit and the resolution ('you can't have a favourite') is both philosophically coherent for Robert and a power-play dismissal. 'Sometimes I feel you don't know food at all' mirrors Angela's line back at Andy, adding a layer. Very Robert.

jokes.text: Gabe awkwardly appears at the warehouse safety meeting and says 'Corporate. Continue.' trying to assert dominance; no one is impressed.
jokes.setup: Gabe has inserted himself into a warehouse safety meeting to be near Val
jokes.punchline: 'Corporate. Continue.' as an authority assertion is immediately deflated by context — he's just a nervous, lovelorn man attending a meeting he has no business at
jokes.explanation: Gabe's entire comic mode is failed authority, and 'Corporate. Continue.' is a crisp expression of that. The warehouse context (where no one respects office people) makes it land harder.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Have I not been a reliable number two?' / Dwight: 'Do not go there.' / Andy: 'You're the deuce I never want to drop.'
jokes.setup: Andy uses 'number two' figuratively to mean second-in-command
jokes.punchline: Dwight recognizes the double meaning and warns against it; Andy goes there anyway with 'deuce I never want to drop' — a toilet metaphor for their working relationship
jokes.explanation: The wordplay on 'number two/deuce' is juvenile but executed with enough self-awareness (Dwight's preemptive warning) to elevate it. Andy's commitment to the metaphor despite the warning is character-appropriate.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'I will do my voodoo.' / Andy: 'Go do the voodoo that you do so we—' / Dwight: 'I will do my voodoo.'
jokes.setup: Andy tries to use the 'voodoo that you do' idiom
jokes.punchline: Dwight refuses to complete the rhyme or engage with Andy's wordplay, flatly restating his own version
jokes.explanation: A quick bit that works on Dwight's literalism and refusal to play along with Andy's enthusiasm. Lightweight but functional.

jokes.text: Gabe to Toby: 'Whom I am seeing is Val, from down in the warehouse. I'm not technically seeing her but I've seen her with the eyes. And there was attraction in at least one direction, so...'
jokes.setup: Gabe is filing pre-emptive workplace relationship paperwork for a woman he has not actually spoken to romantically
jokes.punchline: 'I've seen her with the eyes' and 'attraction in at least one direction' reduce his 'relationship' to its most pathetically minimal definition
jokes.explanation: Strong Gabe characterization — his formal speech patterns ('Whom I am seeing') clashing with the utterly embryonic nature of this 'relationship' is pitch-perfect. 'I've seen her with the eyes' is a great line.

jokes.text: Gabe: 'I don't want a bunch of bureaucratic red tape wrapped around my jock, you know?'
jokes.setup: Gabe is explaining why he wants to file paperwork now before the relationship progresses
jokes.punchline: The grotesquely physical metaphor ('red tape wrapped around my jock') is absurdly mismatched with Gabe's formal, reedy persona
jokes.explanation: The incongruity of Gabe using locker-room language while being the least athletic, most corporate person in the room is the joke. Works on character alone.

jokes.text: Gabe: 'Do you know her last name yet?' / 'Toby, I'm gonna tell you her last name tomorrow because she's gonna be screaming it tonight.' / Toby: 'She's gonna be screaming her own last name?'
jokes.setup: Gabe uses a sexual bravado non-sequitur ('she's gonna be screaming it tonight') implying passion
jokes.punchline: Toby's literal interpretation ('She's gonna be screaming her own last name?') perfectly deflates the bravado by pointing out the logical absurdity
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best constructed jokes. Gabe's bravado is already funny in context, but Toby's literal rejoinder is a perfect comedic deconstruction — pointing out that the idiom doesn't actually make sense when you think about it. It's also a rare Toby win. The structure is flawless: setup, expected punchline subverted, then the actual punchline that reframes everything. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Dwight explains five mistakes = 'a home run' and 'one home run and you're out' — inverting baseball scoring as a negative outcome
jokes.setup: Dwight frames the accountability system in sports metaphors
jokes.punchline: He uses 'home run' as the catastrophic threshold — rewiring the metaphor so sports achievement = workplace disaster
jokes.explanation: The inverted baseball logic is a neat Dwight-ism — he's constructed an elaborate system with its own internal jargon that makes a perverse kind of sense. Mild but consistent with his character.

jokes.text: The office learns the failsafe will also forward every negative email they've ever sent Robert about him. Reading of the emails: 'Creep by TLC, Creep by Radiohead.' / 'There's no way he hasn't strangled at least one stripper.' (Jim) / 'He eats his yogurt like he is punishing it for disappointing him.' (Oscar)
jokes.setup: The team thinks the doomsday device only sends the branch closure report; Dwight reveals it also forwards their personal emails about Robert
jokes.punchline: The escalating email readings reveal increasingly unhinged takes on Robert, with the specificity of each observation being funnier than the last
jokes.explanation: This sequence is beautifully constructed. Each email is character-specific and escalating: Jim's is paranoid-dark ('strangled at least one stripper'), Oscar's is precise and literary ('punishing it for disappointing him'), and Kelly's has the added tag that makes it devastating. The specificity of 'he eats his yogurt like he is punishing it' is the kind of line that becomes a fan favorite — it perfectly captures Robert's intensity while being completely absurd as an observation.

jokes.text: Jim's email about Robert: 'There's no way he hasn't strangled at least one stripper.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is reading embarrassing emails written about Robert
jokes.punchline: Jim's speculation is extreme and specific — 'at least one stripper' implies careful thought about Robert's dark possibilities
jokes.explanation: The precision of 'at least one' does a lot of work. Jim, normally the straight man, has a deliciously dark inner monologue about Robert. The joke is character-consistent (Jim is privately irreverent) and economical. Strong quotability.

jokes.text: Oscar's email: 'He eats his yogurt like he is punishing it for disappointing him.'
jokes.setup: Dwight continues reading embarrassing emails about Robert
jokes.punchline: Oscar's observation is hyper-specific and vivid — it perfectly captures Robert's intensity while revealing that Oscar has been closely watching Robert eat yogurt
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. 'He eats his yogurt like he is punishing it for disappointing him' is a masterclass in comedic description: it tells us everything about Robert California's personality in a single image. The specificity is remarkable — yogurt, not food in general. 'Punishing it for disappointing him' is the perfect verb choice. This is the kind of line that becomes a fan-favorite quote. Clearly one of the episode's top two jokes; compares favorably to the 8.0 benchmark.

jokes.text: Kelly's email PS: 'We should kill him.' / Robert's reaction-beat read as Andy delivers it flatly: 'That's not that bad, actually.'
jokes.setup: The email revelations have been building; Kelly's ends with a casual murder suggestion
jokes.punchline: Andy's delivery of 'That's not that bad, actually' treats murder advocacy as a comparative judgment — implying the other emails were worse
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the email sequence. The economy is nearly flawless — four words that reframe 'PS we should kill him' as comparatively reasonable. The deadpan is the joke.

jokes.text: Jim: 'Wait. So you installed a doomsday device?' / Dwight: 'No, it's an Accountability Booster.' / Jim: 'Which, when it goes off, it destroys everything.' / Dwight: 'Very similar to a doomsday device.'
jokes.setup: Jim cuts through Dwight's corporate euphemism
jokes.punchline: Dwight's reluctant concession — 'very similar to a doomsday device' — is funnier than a flat denial because he almost agrees
jokes.explanation: Classic Jim/Dwight dynamic — Jim names what's really happening, Dwight resists the label, then accidentally confirms it. 'Very similar to a doomsday device' is Dwight's pedantic honesty trumping his desire to spin.

jokes.text: Oscar: 'No, we're not. And you are a psycho who is ruining our lives.'
jokes.setup: Dwight expresses confidence the office is 'equal to the task'
jokes.punchline: Oscar's flat, specific counter — 'you are a psycho who is ruining our lives' — is delivered with the precision of an accountant's assessment
jokes.explanation: Oscar works as a voice of pure reason in Dwight chaos scenes, and 'you are a psycho who is ruining our lives' is a good Oscar line — specific and delivered without affect.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head: 'They're making me out to be a Bond villain. I like to think of myself as a brilliant scientist who will stop at nothing to remake the world. Like — not Doctor Moreau — someone good. Doctor Frankenstein. Doctor Jekyll, not them. Doctor—'
jokes.setup: Dwight rejects the 'Bond villain' label and tries to find a more flattering mad-scientist comparison
jokes.punchline: Every scientist he names is a villain or morally compromised; he can't find one that isn't. The trailing 'Doctor—' implies he's still searching.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully Dwight-specific joke — his self-image is so inflated he needs to find an aspirational mad scientist, but he has enough self-awareness (barely) to rule out the obviously villainous ones, without realizing they're ALL villains. The trailing 'Doctor—' is a perfect structural choice. Strong escalation and character integration.

jokes.text: Ryan's talking head: 'This doomsday device sounds like a scare tactic to me. There's an easy way to tell if this device is a sham — we just make a mistake.'
jokes.setup: Ryan positions himself as too clever to be manipulated by Dwight's device
jokes.punchline: His 'rational' solution (deliberately make a mistake to test the device) is the most catastrophically stupid response possible, framed as logical
jokes.explanation: Ryan's contrarian intelligence-cosplay is his defining trait in later seasons — he's always positioning himself as the smartest in the room while doing something idiotic. This is a clean expression of that.

jokes.text: Warehouse safety meeting: 'Third—' / 'Who knows what the belt is for?' / 'It's for protecting my ass when you suckers lift more than you can handle.'
jokes.setup: Standard workplace safety meeting tone
jokes.punchline: Val's blunt, profanity-laced answer to the rhetorical question immediately establishes her as a no-nonsense straight-shooter
jokes.explanation: Functional character introduction for Val — she's direct and unbothered. Works as establishment comedy rather than a standout gag.

jokes.text: Gabe's talking head: 'I get the sense that Val enjoys a good put-down. Considering that's the only thing I know about her, I will be milking that hard.'
jokes.setup: Gabe is developing a strategy to impress Val based on minimal data
jokes.punchline: His entire romantic strategy consists of one observed trait and a plan to weaponize it — the desperation is naked and precisely articulated
jokes.explanation: 'I will be milking that hard' applied to a romantic strategy based on a single data point is a strong Gabe line. His transparency about his desperation is funny.

jokes.text: Gabe at warehouse meeting: 'The Michelin Man called, he wants his cummerbund back.' [said to Darryl about the support belt]
jokes.setup: Gabe is trying to deploy put-down humor to impress Val
jokes.punchline: The insult is extremely specific, dated, and niche ('cummerbund') — it's so peculiarly Gabe that it's funny as a character joke even if the insult itself doesn't land
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Gabe's version of trash talk involves the word 'cummerbund.' It's a perfect Gabe-specific failure of a burn — technically an insult, but so strange and formal that it baffles rather than roasts.

jokes.text: Oscar's talking head: 'When the stakes are this high, there's only one computer that I trust. And it's powered by Thai food and Spanish reds.'
jokes.setup: Oscar is doing crucial accounting manually under pressure
jokes.punchline: He frames doing math by hand (while eating and drinking) as a principled choice about computer reliability — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Strong economy and quotability. 'Powered by Thai food and Spanish reds' is an excellent line — the specificity of the foods (ethnic food + sophisticated wine = Oscar) makes it character-specific. The straight-faced framing as a principled computing philosophy elevates it.

jokes.text: Jim: 'If this doomsday device goes off—' / Dwight: 'Accountability Booster.' / Jim: 'If this bad idea goes off...'
jokes.setup: Jim keeps using the banned term 'doomsday device'
jokes.punchline: After Dwight corrects him, Jim pivots not to the correct name but to an even more dismissive alternative: 'bad idea'
jokes.explanation: A well-executed escalation of the running naming gag. Jim's replacement term ('bad idea') is more cutting than 'doomsday device' and demonstrates his growing contempt. Good economy.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam trying to guess Dwight's password. Jim: 'Try Mose-1-2-3-4.' / Pam: 'Dwight would never be that obvious. Try something like Z-6-4-$-8.' / Jim: 'Not that exactly, something like that.' / Pam: 'How about Scranton-Strangler-6-6-6?'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are trying to hack the doomsday device by guessing Dwight's password
jokes.punchline: Pam's escalating suggestions reveal she has genuinely internalized Dwight's worldview enough to consider 'Scranton-Strangler-6-6-6' a plausible password — which it probably is
jokes.explanation: A fun Jim/Pam partnership scene. 'Scranton-Strangler-6-6-6' is the best guess because it's so specifically Dwight-plausible — referencing an ongoing show mystery with Dwight's affinity for darkness and the number of the beast. Good escalation.

jokes.text: Jim: 'What's Dwight's mother's name?' / Pam: 'Hedda.' [long pause, they stare at each other]
jokes.setup: Jim asks about Dwight's mother's name as a password guess
jokes.punchline: Pam immediately knows the answer — 'Hedda' — without hesitation, and the pause acknowledges they both know far more about Dwight than is healthy
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely in the reaction beat — Pam's immediate knowledge and the mutual recognition of how deeply Dwight-adjacent their lives have become. Strong visual/silence comedy.

jokes.text: Gabe bribes Val with $100 to get coffee and contrives to go with her, then contradicts himself: 'Don't bring me any of that caramel soy latte crap, okay? I want a decaf frappuccino.' / Val: 'Caramel soy latte.' / Gabe: 'No, a decaf frap.'
jokes.setup: Gabe gives Val instructions after pretending to be generous
jokes.punchline: He tells her not to get a fancy drink then immediately orders one — and then has to correct Val when she repeats back what he said
jokes.explanation: The self-contradiction is a mild cringe joke about Gabe's haplessness. Functional but not particularly sharp — the setup (the $100 bribe, the fake generosity) is more interesting than the coffee punchline.

jokes.text: Andy's reaction to learning five strikes have been reached: 'I was saving this for my retirement, which I guess is today.' [pulls out bottle]
jokes.setup: The office has just hit five mistakes in one day; Andy realizes the doomsday device will fire
jokes.punchline: Andy had a retirement drink prepared — implying he always saw this coming — delivered with defeated calm
jokes.explanation: Good Andy character moment — the detail that he had a retirement drink prepared is both sad and funny, and 'which I guess is today' has good comic timing implied. Solid deadpan.

jokes.text: Kevin: 'Can you tell me now where paper comes from?' / Kevin: 'The man tree puts its penis...' / Andy: 'Okay. All right.'
jokes.setup: Dwight challenges Kevin on the paper-making project he was supposedly working on instead of accounting
jokes.punchline: Kevin's explanation of how paper is made immediately reveals he has learned nothing; 'the man tree puts its penis—' is cut off before completion, which is funnier than finishing it
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes of the episode. Kevin's sexual personification of tree reproduction as his understanding of paper manufacturing is perfectly Kevin — childlike, oblivious, confident. The truncation ('puts its penis—') is a masterstroke of economy; the imagination fills in the rest. Andy's defeated 'Okay. All right.' is the perfect reaction. Highly quotable and completely character-specific.

jokes.text: Dwight's final word to the office as he leaves: 'Good luck finding a new job, idiots. I'll make sure to write you a glowing reference.' / Beat. / 'Glowingly negative.'
jokes.setup: Dwight storms out after refusing to stop the device
jokes.punchline: He offers a 'glowing reference' as a parting gesture — then immediately clarifies it will be glowingly negative, as if he wants credit for technical accuracy
jokes.explanation: 'Glowingly negative' is a strong Dwight line — the pause-and-correction structure, his need to be precise even in the middle of a dramatic exit. Economy and character integration are both high.

jokes.text: Andy's plan: 'Pam, you should come with me. Dwight really likes you, and your breasts are enormous, that could help us.' / Kevin's assignment: 'Kevin has that lovability.'
jokes.setup: Andy is assigning roles for the mission to stop Dwight
jokes.punchline: Andy mentions Pam's breasts as a strategic asset in the same breath as Dwight liking her, with complete managerial sincerity; Kevin's assignment is 'lovability' — the only trait Andy can identify
jokes.explanation: Andy's oblivious HR violation delivered as strategic planning is funny — the 'enormous' adjective is the tell that he's trying to be professional and failing. Pairing it with Kevin's 'lovability' (the most Kevin possible asset) makes the sequence work as a double.

jokes.text: Jim about Robert's location: 'He's at some club where you either eat squash or play squash.' / Jim: 'I'll try both.'
jokes.setup: Jim needs to find Robert California at a club
jokes.punchline: The confusion between the vegetable and the sport is a mild wordplay moment; Jim's 'I'll try both' is a deadpan commitment to covering his bases
jokes.explanation: Lightweight wordplay/deadpan. 'I'll try both' is a good Jim line but the squash-as-vegetable joke is thin setup for it.

jokes.text: Pam arrives at Dwight's farm with a gift, tries to reason with him. Dwight: 'Get lost.' / Pam: 'Well, now hold on.' / Dwight: 'What does it look like I'm doing?' / Pam: 'Digging a grave for a horse.'
jokes.setup: Pam tries to appeal to Dwight at his farm; he's doing something unexpected
jokes.punchline: Pam's matter-of-fact identification of the activity ('digging a grave for a horse') is funny because it's accurate and she says it with zero alarm — she's been normalized to Dwight's world
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of the situation (horse grave) is sold entirely by Pam's flat delivery. Her complete lack of shock is the joke — she's been working with Dwight long enough that 'digging a horse grave' barely registers as unusual.

jokes.text: Dwight digging: 'If you hit another horse, you've dug too far.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is digging a horse grave and Pam and Jim have offered to help
jokes.punchline: Dwight's instructions imply there are multiple horses buried already — this is not a new occurrence on Schrute Farms
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. Pure Dwight — the casual, practical instruction implies a cemetery's worth of buried horses that he's never mentioned. The economy is near-perfect: one sentence, delivered as a digging tip, that reveals an entire dark history. It's highly quotable, deeply character-specific (only Dwight has this problem), and the dark implication (many dead horses) is funny without being explained. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in craft; the character specificity pushes it higher.

jokes.text: Dwight shows Pam and Kevin around the farmhouse: 'This is the newest addition, built by Erasmus Schrute in 1808. It doubled as a tuberculosis recovery room until 2009.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is proudly showing off his farmhouse while they soften him up
jokes.punchline: 'Until 2009' — meaning Dwight was treating tuberculosis patients in his farmhouse addition within recent memory
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in the recency of the date — 'until 2009' takes what sounds like historical color ('built in 1808') and snaps it into the present. The implication that Schrute Farms had an active tuberculosis ward in the 21st century is gloriously dark and completely consistent with the Dwight mythology.

jokes.text: Pam and Kevin discuss Labradoodles: 'That's too much doodle and not enough lab.' / 'Yeah, when are they gonna do a Labradoodle that's just lab? That's what I'm saying.'
jokes.setup: Pam and Kevin are chatting while Dwight leads them around the farm
jokes.punchline: The mundane suburban dog-breed complaint in the middle of a crisis mission is the joke — they've gone completely off-task; also 'a Labradoodle that's just lab' is technically not a Labradoodle
jokes.explanation: Mild observational comedy that works as character business — Pam and Kevin's off-task banter is charming — but the joke itself (Labradoodle breed preference) isn't particularly sharp.

jokes.text: Gabe asks Val to the cemetery for wine: 'Tonight I was thinking I'm gonna go to the cemetery. I'm gonna drink a little wine and I thought maybe you'd like to come with me.'
jokes.setup: Gabe has been building to asking Val out
jokes.punchline: His date pitch is wine at a cemetery — framed as a romantic offer, which is inherently gothic and off-putting from anyone but especially Gabe
jokes.explanation: The cemetery date is so perfectly Gabe — morbid, unaware, strangely formal. Only Gabe would describe this as a date invitation and not understand why it's terrifying. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Val immediately shuts down Gabe: 'Are you asking me on a date?' / Gabe: 'Yes, I am.' / Val: 'Because I don't date coworkers, it's not personal. It's a matter of policy.' / Gabe: 'I could quit.' / Val: 'Don't quit.' / Gabe: 'Good policy. It's sensible. Smart.'
jokes.setup: Val rejects Gabe professionally by citing a no-coworker policy
jokes.punchline: Gabe immediately offers to quit his job, then validates her rejection policy with increasing enthusiasm as a face-saving move ('Good policy. It's sensible. Smart.')
jokes.explanation: Gabe's offer to quit to date Val is peak Gabe desperation, followed by his recovery strategy — enthusiastically endorsing her rejection — which is both sad and funny. 'Don't quit' from Val is perfectly dry.

jokes.text: Jim tries to delay Robert at squash: Robert serves and Jim awkwardly plays. 'All right. Serving. Serving, serving, serving. In the box. In the box.'
jokes.setup: Jim has challenged Robert to squash to keep him away from his phone until 5:00
jokes.punchline: Jim is clearly not a squash player — his narration of 'in the box, in the box' suggests he's trying to remember the rules in real time
jokes.explanation: Functional physical comedy setup. Jim's out-of-his-depth squash playing is situationally funny but the transcript doesn't give us enough to work with beyond the mumbled self-coaching.

jokes.text: Kevin's plan to save the company: 'I know how to save the company, everyone. Just write a petition, get everyone's signatures including our clients, march down to Florida and shove it up your butt.'
jokes.setup: The office is brainstorming how to avert the doomsday device with 15 minutes left
jokes.punchline: Kevin's plan starts as a plausible corporate action (petition, signatures) then pivots to 'march down to Florida and shove it up your butt' — directed at no one in particular
jokes.explanation: Kevin's plan escalates from reasonable to bizarre to hostile with the pivot point being 'Florida' (where Robert's corporate office presumably is). The 'shove it up your butt' isn't specified at whom, which is funnier. Good Kevin energy.

jokes.text: Meredith's flat response to Kevin's plan: 'It's not that funny.'
jokes.setup: Kevin has just delivered his absurd plan
jokes.punchline: Meredith's 'it's not that funny' — presumably said as the group is laughing — is a perfect wet-blanket reaction that's funnier than engagement would be
jokes.explanation: Meredith's deadpan killjoy response is character-appropriate. Four words that deflate a moment — good economy.

jokes.text: Pam distracts Dwight: 'Pam, you got something on your shirt. Oh!' then says 'Pobody's nerfect, right?' — a transposition of 'nobody's perfect'
jokes.setup: Pam is stalling Dwight and apparently spills something on herself in the process of a clumsy diversion
jokes.punchline: 'Pobody's nerfect' — the spoonerism of 'nobody's perfect' — is Pam's awkward attempt to seem casual while managing an awkward situation
jokes.explanation: The spoonerism is a real folk-saying (it exists) so it works on two levels — Pam's awkward deployment of a half-joke phrase, and the audience's recognition of the real saying. Functional.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Did you just have a stroke, Pam? It's nobody's perfect.' / Kevin: 'Nice stroke, Pam.' / Pam: 'No, it's a jokey saying — Pobody's nerfect. Like, I can't even say those words right.'
jokes.setup: Pam tries to explain the spoonerism joke
jokes.punchline: Dwight's literal correction, Kevin's supportive but oblivious 'Nice stroke, Pam,' and Pam's increasingly desperate explanation all miss each other — each character is in their own comedic register
jokes.explanation: The three-way miscommunication is the joke — Dwight's diagnostic literalism, Kevin's misplaced sympathy, and Pam's flustered explanation. 'Nice stroke, Pam' from Kevin is the standout beat.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'You know what would go so great with this cabbage pie? Milk.' / Pam: 'Any specific animal?' / Dwight: 'I'm thinking cow.' / Kevin: 'Don't say cow.'
jokes.setup: They're sitting in Dwight's farmhouse; Dwight mentions cabbage pie
jokes.punchline: Pam's 'Any specific animal?' is a sharp callback to Schrute Farm's animal diversity; Kevin's 'Don't say cow' implies he has some complicated relationship with cows (or just doesn't want milk)
jokes.explanation: A quick three-beat exchange that works. 'Any specific animal?' is a great Pam line — she's learned to ask for specificity at Schrute Farms. Kevin's 'Don't say cow' is delightfully unexplained.

jokes.text: Pam's stalling goodbye: 'Thanks for everything. Sive drafely.' / Dwight: 'Wasn't it supposed to be drive safely?'
jokes.setup: Pam is trying to stall Dwight with small talk as they leave; she botches the farewell
jokes.punchline: Another Pam spoonerism/mangling — this time accidental — and Dwight immediately notices and corrects it, even as she's trying to manipulate him
jokes.explanation: A callback to the spoonerism gag, but this one is genuine nervous slip rather than deployed phrase. Dwight's correction is funny because he's focusing on the wrong thing entirely — grammar over the manipulation attempt happening right in front of him.

jokes.text: Jim's phone battle with Robert at squash: Jim tries to check Robert's phone, they tussle over it, Jim drops it, Robert: 'What the *?' / Jim: 'Oh man, I'm sorry!' / Robert: 'Jesus! Did it break?' / Jim: 'No it's good, thanks.'
jokes.setup: Jim needs to intercept the email on Robert's phone; he's been trying to grab it subtly
jokes.punchline: The phone struggle devolves into open chaos — Jim drops the phone, there's a near-disaster, and Jim immediately thanks Robert for the phone surviving as if Robert was doing him a favor
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy that works better on screen than in transcript. The beats are functional but relatively standard sitcom physical gag. 'No it's good, thanks' is a good Jim deflection.

jokes.text: Robert and Jim examine each other's phones after the melee: 'What kind of iPhone is that?' / 'It's the standard one, the one everyone has.' / 'Yeah, I have the one that nobody has.'
jokes.setup: They've just had a physical altercation over phones and are now calmly comparing devices
jokes.punchline: Robert has a rare/prototype iPhone — 'the one that nobody has' — delivered as a completely ordinary statement, consistent with his character as someone always operating at a different level
jokes.explanation: Robert's 'I have the one that nobody has' is perfectly in character — he naturally has access to things others don't, mentioned without pride or explanation. The mundane delivery of an extraordinary claim is his comedic signature.

jokes.text: Robert reads Jim's email notifications: 'Is there anything interesting? It depends, Jim. Do you find one-day-only JetBlue sales to Buffalo interesting?'
jokes.setup: Robert has Jim's phone and is reading his emails
jokes.punchline: The mundanity of Jim's inbox (JetBlue sales to Buffalo) is contrasted with the high stakes of the situation — Robert's dry narration of Jim's boring email life is a power move
jokes.explanation: Robert's clinical reading of Jim's discount airline emails is funny because of the specificity ('Buffalo') and the power dynamic — the CEO reading the assistant's spam. 'It depends, Jim' as an opener is excellent.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head after squash: 'Well, I am sore and obviously horrible at this.'
jokes.setup: Jim has just played squash against Robert California as a stalling tactic
jokes.punchline: His self-assessment is delivered with the exhausted resignation of someone who gave 100% and still failed athletically
jokes.explanation: Mild Jim talking head. Self-deprecating and functional but thin — doesn't add much beyond what we've seen.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head after canceling the device — discussing the office: 'They're not my favorite people in the world. I wouldn't even call them friends. They come over here, eat my pie, dig the crappiest horse grave you've ever seen.' / Beat. / 'God, I'm gonna have to work with them forever, aren't I?'
jokes.setup: Dwight has just relented and cancelled the doomsday device after Pam and Kevin came to his farm
jokes.punchline: 'The crappiest horse grave you've ever seen' is unexpected specificity; 'I'm gonna have to work with them forever, aren't I?' reframes the whole emotional arc as Dwight's reluctant acknowledgment of connection — disguised as a complaint
jokes.explanation: A beautiful episode button. 'The crappiest horse grave you've ever seen' calls back to the farm scene and lands as a high bar for a bad horse grave — implying Dwight has comparative data. But 'God, I'm gonna have to work with them forever, aren't I?' is the real emotional punchline — it's Dwight's version of an expression of affection, and it's genuinely touching while being funny. This is The Office at its best: comedy that earns an emotional beat.

jokes.text: Jim and Robert California play squash; Jim falls and skins his knee. They both agree it hurts and carry on.
jokes.setup: Jim has been playing squash with Robert to keep him occupied, despite not being a squash player
jokes.punchline: Jim falls, both men have a surprisingly candid exchange about how much it hurts, then immediately resume playing — the normality of the interaction after the episode's tension is the joke
jokes.explanation: A mild physical coda. The joke is partly structural — the episode's big drama has been resolved and we end on something mundane. Not a strong standalone joke but it serves the episode's rhythm. Below average craft; the laughs come from context rather than writing.

tmdb_overview: Dwight installs a Doomsday device that will fire all of the employees and effectively close down the branch if they make too many mistakes. Meanwhile, Gabe attempts to court the new warehouse worker, Val.
